t: burnt offering. Its laws will be explained below in chapter 6.
and sin offering. Its laws will be explained below in chapter 7.
and guilt offering. Its laws will be explained below in 9:1-2.
and peace offerings. Their laws will be explained below in 9:4-8.
the Pesach offering. The Pesach offering slaughtered on the fourteenth of Nisan (Hilchot Korban Pesach 1:1).
and the firstborn. The firstborn of a pure animal (Hilchot Bechorot 1:2).
and the tithe. The animal tithe (ibid. 6:4). The offering rite of the three of them appears below in 9:25.

from the two lambs that come with the wave bread on Shavuot. Two lambs that came on Shavuot and were waved together with the two loaves, and afterward were slaughtered and offered on the altar (Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 8:11).
the two daily tamid offerings. Two lambs offered every day for the tamid offering, one in the morning and one in the afternoon (Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 1:1).

and the additional offerings of Sabbaths, new moons and festivals. Offerings in addition to the tamid, which were offered on Sabbaths and festivals and are mentioned in the portion of Pinchas in the Book of Numbers.
and the goat sin offering of Yom Kippur. See ibid. 10:2, Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:3.
and they ruled regarding idolatry. That it is permitted to worship it, and the people worshipped according to their ruling (Hilchot Shegagot 12:1).
and they ruled regarding the other commandments. They permitted one of the prohibitions for which one is liable to karet, and the people transgressed that commandment according to their ruling.
as will be explained. There.

and the festival offering, which is a peace offering, and the appearance offering, which is burnt offerings. A peace offering and a burnt offering brought on each festival when going up on pilgrimage (Hilchot Chagigah 1:1).
and the offering of a convert etc.. The offering brought by a gentile who converts as part of the process of his conversion (see also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 13:4-5, Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:2).
and one who vows or donates a burnt offering or peace offerings. Different ways in which a person obligates himself to bring an offering to the Temple (see below 14:4).
and peace offerings that come with the bread are called a thanksgiving offering. See below 9:5.
and likewise the offerings of the nazirite. Which the nazirite brings when he completes his days of nezirut (see Hilchot Nezirut 8:1).
and the offerings of the leper. Which he brings after completing his purification process (Hilchot Shegagot 10:3).
and the offerings of zavim and women after childbirth. Which they bring after completing their purification process (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 1:3).
and it is a sin offering. See Hilchot Shegagot 1:1 (and there are several sins for which one brings an ascending and descending sin offering - ibid. 10:1).
he brings a guilt offering, and this is called a conditional guilt offering. Ibid. 8:1.
and there are transgressions for which he brings a guilt offering, and this is called a definite guilt offering. See ibid. 9:1.
and likewise the ram of the burnt offering and the bull of the sin offering that the High Priest offers from his own on Yom Kippur. See Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:1.

he is responsible for them and for the responsibility of their libations. The libations are the fine flour, oil and wine that come with the offering (below 2:1). If the offering or the libations that come with it were lost, the owner must bring another offering or libations.
except for a freewill offering. When he donated an animal for an offering, he is not obligated to bring another if it was lost (below 14:5).

and all communal offerings are not subject to responsibility for them nor responsibility for their libations. If they set aside an animal for a communal offering and the time of its offering passed, they are not obligated to offer it and bring its libations.

and if the sacrifice was offered, they are responsible for their libations. When they offered the sacrifice at its time and did not bring libations with it, the community must offer its libations even after its time has passed.
and an individual's offering that has a fixed time. That has a specific date for its offering, such as the bull and ram that the High Priest brings on Yom Kippur.
and he is not responsible for it. He is not obligated to offer it after its time.
and in them, male and female are equal. In the bird offering there is no difference between male and female (see also Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:1).
there is a guilt offering that comes from the larger of this kind and there is a guilt offering that comes from the smaller ones. See Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:22.
from the age of eight days. And before that they are disqualified (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:8).
until a full year, from day to day. From the day of birth until the same date arrives a year later.

if the year was intercalated, it was intercalated for it. And it is considered young until the end of the year according to the date on which it was born, even though twelve months have already passed.

one does not initially offer them except from the thirtieth day onward. For the Torah says regarding offerings, "from the eighth day onward it shall be accepted" (Leviticus 22:27), and from this they learned that initially one should not offer them on the eighth day but only at a later time.

except for the firstborn... that if he wished to offer them on the eighth day initially, he offers. For regarding the firstborn it says, "on the eighth day you shall give it to Me" (Exodus 22:29), and from this it follows that it may be offered even initially on the eighth day, and from it they learned regarding the tithe and the Pesach offering (Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 1:4).
these are yearlings. Until the end of their first year.
two-year-olds. Until the age of two years.
but on the thirtieth day. And likewise from the end of the first year until the thirtieth day.
a palgas. The meaning of the word in Greek: a youth who is no longer a child and not yet an adult (and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 1:3).
a two-year-old bull. From its second year it is called a bull. But it may be offered until the end of three years as above in halachah 11 (Kesef Mishneh).
every second year it is called a goat. From the beginning of the year to its end (unlike a ram - Mirkevet HaMishneh).
and all communal sin offerings are from goats. The idolatry goat of the community and the goats of new moons and festivals.
or from cattle. The bull for an unwitting communal error.
from lambs and from cattle. The tamid and additional offerings that come from lambs, from rams and from cattle.
except for three sin offerings. That come from males or from cattle.
the sin offering of a nasi, which is a goat. A male (a goat), which the king brings when he sins in a sin for which an individual brings a sin offering (Hilchot Shegagot 15:1).
and the sin offering of the anointed kohen. Which the High Priest brings when he errs in a ruling and transgresses a commandment for which one is liable to a sin offering (ibid.).
the bull that the High Priest brings on Yom Kippur. Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:1.

from the goat of Yom Kippur whose counterpart is sent away. The sin offering goat that is the partner of the goat sent to Azazel. But the sin offering goat that was offered with the additional offerings is eaten (Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:1).
sacrifices. Offerings from living animals.
most holy offerings... lesser holy offerings. They differ from each other in the place of slaughter (below 5:2-4) and in the laws of eating (below 10:3-7).
the fat that is on the loins. The fat in the place where the hip bones join the pelvic bones.
and the lobe of the liver etc.. A piece of liver projecting from the lower end of the liver that looks like a finger, together with a little of the liver itself.
the whole fat tail. The entire thick tail full of fat found in sheep.

with the vertebrae of the spine up to the place of the kidneys. The vertebrae of the spine enter into the fat tail; when the fat tail is removed, all the vertebrae in it must be removed with it, together with the vertebrae above it up to above the kidneys.
the kidneys. The kidneys.
the limbs that are burned on the altar from the sin offerings that are eaten etc.. In contrast, the flesh of the burnt offering and of the sin offerings that are burned was burned entirely.
the fat on the innards, including the fat on the abomasum. The fat covering the rumen and the reticulum, the omasum and the abomasum (see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 7:6).

even though the months of the fetus were completed. The months of its pregnancy were completed. In this case its fat is forbidden for eating (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 7:3), and nevertheless it need not be offered.
and even if it was found alive. After its mother was slaughtered.
for the fetus is like one of its limbs. It is eaten like the rest of its limbs (see Hilchot Temurah 4:3).
it requires neither waving nor bringing near nor frankincense. Acts that are done with the various meal offerings (see below 12:6-7).
requires salt. Sprinkling salt before burning it on the altar (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:11).
and one does not place it on the fire. On the arrangement of fire on the top of the altar.

and he pours onto the base and it goes down to the shittin. He would pour the wine at the top of the altar, and from there it went down to the base of the altar and from it to the shittin (Rikvu and Lechem Mishneh based on what is said below 7:10; and see Raavad and Kesef Mishneh).
to the shittin. To the holes in the southwest corner of the base (see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 2:11).
the lamb of a woman after childbirth and the ram of the High Priest. Which are obligations and are not a vow or a freewill offering.
and the ram of the High Priest. The ram for a burnt offering that the High Priest brings on Yom Kippur, in addition to the bull of the sin offering (Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 1:1).

except for the sin offering of the leper and his guilt offering. The leper brings on the day of his purification a sin offering, a guilt offering and a burnt offering (above 1:6), and with his three offerings he brings libations (below halachah 6).
whose libations were specified in the Torah. Leviticus 14:10.
as it is said: to fulfill a vow etc.. Regarding the obligation of libations.
to bring peace offerings of the festival and the burnt offering of appearance. Although it is obligatory to offer them on the festival (Hilchot Chagigah 1:1), libations must be brought with them.
a lamb or a ewe lamb. Young ones, in their first year.
an issaron... the hin. See below, halachah 7.
the libations of a ewe. A ewe in its second year.
a ram. A lamb in its second year.
for each and every one. For each and every offering, even when he brings many offerings.

from the lamb of the burnt offering that is offered on the day of the waving of the omer. Which was offered on the second day of Pesach together with the omer meal offering (Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 7:3).
that its libations are two issaronim mixed with a third of a hin of oil. Double the libations of a lamb.
its wine was not doubled; rather, wine for the libation is a quarter of a hin. Like the libations of other lambs.
and from oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
the palgas. A lamb in the first month of its second year, which is fit neither as a lamb nor as a ram (above 1:14).
and we have already made known the measure of the log along with other measures in Hilchot Eruvin. 1:13; and in today's measures the log is about 350 cc.
and the issaron is the omer. And its measure is a tenth of an ephah (Exodus 16:36).
and we have already explained its measure in the matter of challah. Hilchot Bikkurim 6:15; and there it says that its measure is forty-three and a fifth eggs (about 2.5 liters).
with one issaron that was in the Temple. A measuring vessel in the Temple for dry measure, with which they measured the fine flour for meal offerings (Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 1:16).

the oil of libations is measured by its measure in the Temple. Each libation in the appropriate vessel of the liquid measures that were in the Temple: a quarter of a hin for a lamb, a third of a hin for a ram, half a hin for a bull (ibid. 1:17).

and the oil of an individual's meal offerings in the log in the Temple. A meal offering that an individual donates to the altar is no less than one issaron of fine flour, and he may add to it as much as he wishes (below 12:5). For each issaron one must give a log of oil (ibid. halachah 7), and this log was measured with a log measure that was in the Temple.
the number of issaronim is the number of logs. According to the number of issaronim of fine flour, so is the number of logs of oil.
the overflows of the measures. What rises and heaps above the height of the vessel.
the back of the issaron. The outer side of the vessel.
as we have explained. Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 1:19.
even though the intention of the measurer is only for what is inside the vessel. And service vessels sanctify only when one intends that they sanctify (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 3:20).

lest they say: they take out from a service vessel to unconsecrated use. For one who sees knows that the liquid measures were anointed on the outside as well, and does not know that the measurer intended only what is inside, and will think that it is permitted to treat as unconsecrated what was sanctified in a service vessel.
if there is another sacrifice there, they are offered with it. If there is another offering there that requires libations, they offer the overflows as the libations of that offering.

and if not, they are disqualified by being left overnight. If they were not used for the libations of other offerings, they are disqualified after a night, like everything sanctified in a sacred vessel (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 3:18).

and if not, they use them to "summer" the altar. If they have not yet been disqualified by being left overnight, they can be redeemed and the money used to buy offerings for the "summer of the altar" - communal freewill burnt offerings that were offered in addition to the obligatory offerings (and so called after the summer fruits that come as an addition to a meal - Commentary on the Mishnah, Shekalim 4:4).
how. Do they "summer" the altar?
they buy with them. They sell the overflows and with the money they receive they buy offerings and offer them as burnt offerings.
and the hides belong to the kohanim. Like the other hides of burnt offerings (below 5:19).
the fine flour with the oil of libations does not hold up the wine, nor does the wine hold them up. And he may bring one even if he does not bring the other.
if they were left overnight, they are disqualified. And he must bring other libations.
libations are brought only from unconsecrated funds. For the reason for this law see below 16:17.
a thanksgiving offering whose bread he brings from the tithe. When he stipulated that he would bring it so, he may bring it from the money of second tithe (ibid.).
the libations mentioned in the Book of Ezekiel. Chapters 45-46.
inauguration offerings. Offerings that come for the dedication of the service in the Temple.

that the princes offered at the dedication of the altar. The twelve princes of the tribes offered offerings each day at the dedication of the Tabernacle in the days of Moses our teacher (Numbers chapter 7).
and they offered on the Sabbath. For they offered for twelve consecutive days.
so too the prince will offer his dedication offering on the Sabbath in the future, as is explained there. Ezekiel 46:4.
those who came from captivity. The people who went up with Ezra from the exile (see Ezra 8:35).
but things that apply for generations. The measure of the libations.
are the words of Torah that we have explained. Above, halachot 4-6.
whether by vow or by freewill offering. Different ways in which a person obligates himself to bring an offering to the Temple (see below 14:4).
and even a bird may come in partnership. But a meal offering does not come in partnership (below 14:2).

and from the hand of a foreigner you shall not offer the bread of your God from any of these. The passage there deals with an animal with a blemish. And it says that it should not be accepted from gentiles as an offering, from which it follows that when it has no blemish a gentile may offer it (Yerushalmi, Avodah Zarah 2:1). And from the fact that the beginning of the passage deals with a burnt offering (Leviticus 22:18), we learn that only a burnt offering is accepted from a gentile (Babylonian Talmud, Menachot 73b).
even though he worships idols. And we are not concerned that he may have brought this offering for the sake of idolatry (Radbaz).
and likewise burnt offerings that do not come by vow or freewill offering. For the passage there deals with offerings that come by vow and by freewill offering.
who brought peace offerings. He brought an offering for the sake of peace offerings.
his heart is toward Heaven. And not that people should eat from it.
on condition that atonement be made with them for Israel. That an Israelite who was obligated to bring peace offerings fulfilled his obligation with them.
an Israelite who is a meshumad etc.. See also Hilchot Shegagot 3:7.
a meshumad for idolatry. One accustomed to worship idols at any time (see Hilchot Teshuvah 3:9).
publicly. Openly.
from oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
whether to provoke. He transgresses the prohibition out of contempt and rebellion.
or for appetite. He transgresses this prohibition because of his desire and not as rebellion.
the native-born. An Israelite.

but their libations are offered from the community's funds. Although the gentiles themselves do not bring their libations, their offering requires libations, and these must be bought from communal funds (see also Hilchot Shekalim 4:3, and in the rulings and opinions here).
semichah. Explained in the following halachot.

all money whose law is that it falls into the freewill offering chests etc.. The money remaining from what a person set aside for his offering is put into the collection chests in the Temple, and burnt offerings are bought with it (Hilchot Shekalim 2:2-3; and see also Hilchot Temurah 4:5).

and if he was a kohen, its service and its hide belong to the men of the watch. Ordinarily a kohen who brings an offering is entitled to offer it himself, to eat its meat (in offerings that are eaten) and to receive its hide (see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:7). However, burnt offerings offered with the money placed in the freewill offering chests are considered communal, and therefore even if the burnt offering was bought with a kohen's money, the offering of the burnt offering and its hide belong to the men of the kohanim's watch serving in the Temple that week.
the agent. One who offers an animal on behalf of another.
who died and left his offering as a burnt offering or peace offerings. But if he left a sin offering or a guilt offering, they are not offered (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 4:1, 4:14).
on the goat that is sent away. To Azazel on Yom Kippur, the High Priest leans on it (Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 4:2).
and on the bull of an unwitting communal error. The bull for an unwitting communal error (see above 1:5).
and he must lean with all his strength. Like all semichah (below halachah 13).

and if the impure person leaned, he leaned. When he put in his hands (or entered in violation) and leaned with all his strength, the semichah counts and he need not lean again (Rikvu, Lechem Mishneh, and see Kesef Mishneh).
the remnants of the commandment. And it is not the essence of the commandment.
if he did not lean, it atones. The offering is valid.

and nevertheless it is counted against him as if it did not atone. He did not perform the commandment in the best manner (Rashi, Menachot 93b), or it means that he has no reward for bringing the offering (Aruch HaShulchan 68:19).
and not on the sides. The sides of the head.
in the north. The area north of the altar, where the most holy offerings are slaughtered (below 5:2).
and his face to the west etc.. The animal's face toward the Sanctuary, and the one leaning stands east of the animal facing the Sanctuary.

over a sin offering the sin of a sin offering, and over a guilt offering the sin of a guilt offering. He specifies in the confession the sin for which he brings the offering (see also Hilchot Teshuvah 1:1).
and over the burnt offering he confesses the sin of a positive commandment. That he neglected a positive commandment.

and the sin of a negative commandment that was converted to a positive commandment. A negative commandment for which there is an explicit command to correct the transgression by a specific act, whereby it was transferred to be a positive commandment, and one does not receive lashes for it (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2). The burnt offering atones for these sins (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 36a).
I have sinned. Unwittingly.
I have done wrong. Intentionally.
I have transgressed. Denial and great transgressions that involve rebellion against God and casting off the yoke (Commentary on the Mishnah, Yoma 4:2).
and this is my atonement. This offering.
peace offerings. Their slaughter is anywhere in the court (below 5:2).

that he does not confess over peace offerings. For it does not come for a sin, like the other offerings. Therefore it is beloved before the Holy One, blessed be He, and makes peace (the word shelamim) between Israel and their Father in Heaven (Tanchuma, Tzav 7).
the slaughtering. The slaughter.
the offering. The throwing of the blood on the altar.
and once the sun has set, the blood is disqualified. And it may not be thrown on the altar, and the offering is disqualified (see also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 1:37).
whose permitting rites were offered. For the blood that permits the burning of the sacrificial parts and the limbs of the burnt offering on the altar was thrown on the altar.
their sacrificial parts. See above 1:18.
until the dawn rises. The beginning of the lightening of the eastern sky before sunrise (about an hour and a fifth before it - Commentary on the Mishnah, Berakhot 1:1).
and in order to keep far from negligence etc.. So that they not come to burn after dawn (for this principle see below 10:8, Hilchot Kriat Shema 1:9, Hilchot Korban Pesach 8:15).
until midnight. The middle of the night (see also Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 1:6).
knowingly. Intentionally.

they override the Sabbath at their time etc.. The limbs and fats of offerings that were offered on the Sabbath are burned that same day, although their burning could be postponed until after the Sabbath.
the kometz and the. frankincense
. The part of the meal offerings that is offered, from those that are eaten.
and the meal offerings that are burned. The meal offering of a kohen and the meal offering of libations.
at sunset. Close to sunset.
they are consumed. They finish the process of their burning.
like the limbs of a burnt offering. Which may be burned all night.
the libations that come with the sacrifice. Fine flour and wine offered with the offering (above 2:1), and brought together with the offering.
the libations that come by themselves. That he did not bring the libations with the offering but after some time (above 2:12).
he sanctifies them and offers them at night. It is permitted to place them in service vessels so that they be sanctified at night and offer them at night.
for semichah. Above 3:6.
and for melikah. Slaughtering bird offerings with the fingernail (below 6:23).
and for burning. Burning the kometz of the meal offering.
for hagashah. Bringing the meal offering near to the southwest horn of the altar (below 12:6).
and for sprinkling. Sprinkling the blood.
and for waving. Waving the meal offerings or the offerings that require waving.
and for kemitzah. Taking the handful from the meal offering, which is offered (below 12:9, 13:13).

and for the offering of the additional offerings. Offering the additional offerings (but offering the tamid offerings is not valid all day; the morning one is in the morning hours and the afternoon one in the afternoon hours).
and the whole night is valid for burning sacrificial parts and limbs. Of the offerings that were offered during the day.
and nevertheless the zealous hasten to the commandments. And do not wait for the end of the day and night (see also Hilchot Milah 1:8).
with a knife from the service vessels. With a metal knife from the vessels designated for Temple service that were consecrated for that purpose.
with the hard shell of a reed. The hard peel of the reed (see Hilchot Shechitah 1:14).

if he received less of their blood than enough for sprinkling etc.. After the slaughter one must receive the blood in a vessel, and the vessel must contain no less than the amount fit for sprinkling on the altar (see below 5:9).
and he must intend to receive all the blood. Initially one should try to receive all the blood in the vessel.

and he brings the windpipe and gullet and the veins into the basin. He stretches the signs of slaughter (the windpipe and the gullet) and the blood vessels in the neck over the basin so that all the blood enters the vessel.
the basin. A vessel with a pointed bottom used for receiving the blood.
two or most of two. Initially he should cut both signs, and if he cut most of both signs, his slaughter is valid (Hilchot Shechitah 1:9).
so that the blood not run down off it. So that the blood stuck to the knife does not enter the basin.
and blood on the knife he wipes off on the rim of the basin. On its outer side.
the air space of a vessel is like the vessel. And blood received in it is sanctified like blood received in the vessel.

if he was receiving the blood and the bottom of the basin was pierced etc.. If the blood reached the air space of the vessel's walls after its bottom was pierced, it is not sanctified, because at the time it arrived there it was not going to rest there but to fall (and in a case where the bottom of the vessel was pierced after the blood reached the walls of the vessel, the blood was sanctified, even though the blood did not rest in the vessel at all - Radbaz).
for the sake of the sacrifice. For the offering for whose sake it was consecrated: a peace offering for the sake of a peace offering, a burnt offering for the sake of a burnt offering, etc.
and for the sake of its owners. For the sake of the owners of the offering.
at the time of slaughter. At the time of the slaughtering.

that the slaughter be with the other four services. Receiving, sprinkling and carrying, which together with the slaughter are the four services that disqualify the offering by thought (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 13:4).

and if he slaughtered and performed the other services without specification... they are valid and count for the owners. Since an unspecified service in offerings is for the sake of that sacrifice and for the sake of the owners (Babylonian Talmud, Zevachim 2b).
and for the sake of the one offering. The owner.
and that he burn it as fire offerings. That they bring it up to be burned in the fire of the altar.
and that its burning be only for a pleasing aroma. And not as food for the Holy One, blessed be He, and the altar (Aruch HaShulchan 70:15).
as we have explained. Above, halachah 10.
we have already explained that the slaughter of consecrated items is valid by non-kohanim. Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 9:6.
and from the receiving of the blood onward is a commandment of the priesthood. See also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 1:22.
most holy offerings... lesser holy offerings. See above 1:17.
in the north of the altar. The area in the court north of the altar, from the eastern wall of the court to the wall of the Sanctuary.
in every place whose boundaries we explained at the beginning of this book. Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:15-16.

and just as the sin offering is called most holy, so the burnt offering is most holy. The sin offering and guilt offering are called most holy in the Torah (Leviticus 6:18; 7:1), and since the burnt offering has the same laws, it too is considered most holy.
and you shall make one he-goat for a sin offering. And the verse continues: "and two yearling lambs for a sacrifice of peace offerings."
behind the Sanctuary. West of the wall of the Sanctuary there were eleven cubits considered part of the area of the Temple court (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:12).
and if he slaughtered them in the Sanctuary, they are valid. And in a time of need it is permitted to do so even ab initio (Commentary on the Mishnah, Zevachim 6:1).
for the roofs are not fit for slaughter at all. For the roofs were not sanctified (see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 6:7).
before the doors of the Sanctuary were opened. In the morning (Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 6:1; likewise when he slaughtered at another time when the doors were closed).
but the curtain that is on it. When it is closed.
from the middle of the altar downward. Below the "red line" that was at the middle of the height of the altar (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 2:9).

he goes around the corners like the shape of a gamma. The blood is thrown on the two walls of the altar on both sides of the corner. In this way the blood spreads over the altar in the shape of the Greek letter gamma, whose shape is: Γ.
around. From all directions.
and the same applies to the guilt-offering. Of it too it says "around" (Leviticus 7:2).
and the remainder of the blood. The blood that remained in the basin after the two sprinklings.
placings. Applications.
the corners of the outer altar. The angles descending from the corners of the altar (and not the square horns located at the four corners of the altar's top).
he carries it to the altar. As explained below in halakhah 10.
to the thumb. To the thumb.

and he supports his finger with his thumb on one side and the forefinger on the other. He supports the finger that has the blood on it from both sides in order to aim the application exactly at the corner (Radbaz).
and he smears it and goes down opposite the edge of the horn. He smears the blood on his finger from top to bottom along the corner of the altar.
next to the horn, one cubit on this side or on that side. In the cubit adjacent to the corner on both sides.
he wipes his finger on the rim of the basin. He cleans the remains of blood off his finger on the outer edge of the basin.
and there must be enough blood there for dipping etc.. There must be enough blood to dip the finger in it without having to wipe the blood off the sides of the vessel.

and on the base of that horn at which he completed the applications etc.. After completing the application of the blood, he goes down from the surrounding ledge to the floor of the Temple court (on the ramp facing the base, see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 2:14) and pours out the remaining blood on the southern base next to the place where he came down.
the sin-offerings that are burned. See above 1:15-16.
their blood is brought inside the Sanctuary. Their blood is brought into the Sanctuary in order to sprinkle from it there.
as is explicit in the Torah. The bull of the anointed priest, Leviticus 4:5-7; the bull for an unwitting communal error, ibid. 4:16-18; the bull and goat of Yom Kippur, ibid. 16:14-19.
which he meets first when he leaves the Sanctuary. For the Sanctuary is west of the altar.
and where is the sprinkling from their blood done. In what place in the Sanctuary.
between the poles. Between the two poles of the Ark in the Holy of Holies.
on the curtain. On the outer side of the curtain separating the Holy from the Holy of Holies.

on the four horns of the golden altar in the Sanctuary. On the corners of the incense altar (and it seems that here the square horns at the four corners of the altar's top are meant, see below halakhah 14).
on the middle of this altar. The middle of its top.
as will be explained in Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim. 3:5, 4:2.
and if he did not aim the sprinklings inside, they are valid. He was not precise in the direction of their sprinkling.
bulls that are burned and goats that are burned. See above 1:16.
when he enters. The priest who sprinkles in the Sanctuary.

between the altar and the lamp, with the altar in front of him. The priest stood east of the golden altar, at its southeast corner, opposite the space between the altar and the lamp (the golden altar stood in the middle of the Sanctuary, and the lamp was drawn toward the south wall west of the altar). Compare Hilchot Avodat Yom HaKippurim 4:2.
and he places on the horns of the altar on the outside. On the outer side of the projections on the top of the altar.
the bull of the anointed priest, which comes for all the commandments. See above 1:15.
the goats of idolatry. See above 1:16.
the Torah does not specify for them how their blood is applied or where it is applied. See Numbers 15:24-25.
the sin-offering of the congregation. The communal sin-offering brought by the community for a sin when most of them sinned.
for the applications of blood. That they sprinkle from their blood in the Sanctuary on the curtain and on the horns of the golden altar.
and for burning. That their flesh be burned.
and to make the one who burns impure. The one who burns the sin-offerings that are burned, and one who assists in their burning, becomes impure along with his clothes (Hilchot Parah 5:4).
the firstborn, the tithe and the Passover offering. See above 1:6.
one application. One application of blood on the altar.
by pouring opposite the base. He stands near the altar at one of its corners and pours the blood directly on the base (see Rashi, Zevachim 37a).
for the southeast corner had no base, as we have explained. Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 2:10.
he throws. One application.
from oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
their sacrificial fats. See above 1:18.
their skin and their flesh etc.. It is said of the bull and goat of Yom Kippur: "and they shall burn in fire their skins, their flesh".
and he tears open and removes the sacrificial fats. He tears open the animal's belly to take out the sacrificial fats.
most holy offerings... lesser sacrifices. Above 1:17.

the skin of the burnt-offering that he offered. The skin of the burnt-offering belongs to the priest who offers it, and from it they learned that the skins of the other offerings that are most holy also (belong to the priests) (Mishnah, Zevachim 12:3).
and any burnt-offering whose flesh the altar did not acquire. That is, the sacrifice was disqualified before the sprinkling of the blood, before the flesh was fit for burning on the altar.
all most holy offerings etc.. See also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:9.

all most holy offerings in which a disqualification occurred before they were flayed, their skins do not go to the priests. Rather the sacrifice is burned with its skin, even though at the time of the sprinkling of the blood the sacrifice was valid.
after they were flayed, their skins go to the priests. For the altar acquired their flesh by the sprinkling of the blood.
the men of the watch divide them etc.. The priests serving in the Temple that week would divide among themselves the skins of all the sacrifices every week on Friday.

one who dedicates his burnt-offering to the upkeep of the Temple. If one consecrates his burnt-offering for the needs of the Temple, its value is given to the Temple upkeep and the animal is offered as it was originally to be offered (Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 6:8).

and among them were males that by law should be offered as burnt-offerings. When he consecrated all his property, animals fit for sacrifice are not given to the Temple upkeep, but the animals fit for it are offered as burnt-offerings (see also there 5:7, and see Lechem Mishneh, who discusses the relation between the two halakhot).
the skins are sold and the proceeds go to the Temple upkeep. The money from their sale is given to the Temple upkeep.
according to its law as written in the Torah. Leviticus chapter 1.
he slaughters and sprinkles the blood as we have explained. Above 5:2, 5:6.
and flays. The skin.
and cuts up. Cuts and separates the limbs.

the wool on the heads of sheep and the hair on the beards of goats. For the skin of the head of a burnt-offering is not flayed together with the rest of the skin (below halakhah 5), and therefore the hair remains on it (Rashi, Zevachim 85b).
and the hooves. The hooves of the foot.
when they are attached. To the flesh.
and if they came off, they are not brought up. And it is forbidden to bring them up (and see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 3:16).
"your burnt-offerings, the flesh and the blood". And not the other parts of the animal.
and all that burst off the altar, he does not return. If they brought them up to the altar and they were thrown off the altar by the heat of the fire, they do not return them to the altar.
an ember. A glowing piece of wood from the fire pile.
if they have substance. They have flesh that was not burned.
even if they burst off after midnight. Although limbs are not to be burned ab initio after midnight (above 4:2), limbs that were already on the altar and burst off must be returned.
they have no substance. Their flesh was completely burned and turned to ash.
the flesh became charred and dried on them like wood. The flesh on the limbs dried out completely from the fire but did not turn to ash.
and they salt them there. For all sacrifices must be salted (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:11).
and he removes the sciatic nerve. The inner nerve close to the bone on the animal's hip joint. This nerve is forbidden to eat (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 8:1), and it is not burned on the altar.
the ashes in the middle of the altar. The ash of the limbs that were burned, gathered in the middle of the altar.
and he throws all the limbs onto the fire. He would throw the limbs from the end of the ramp onto the fire pile on the altar (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 2:13; and see Mishneh LaMelekh and Even HaAzel).
and after he throws them, he again arranges them on the fire. After the limbs were thrown onto the altar, they are arranged on the large fire pile on the altar.
they do not produce a pleasing aroma. When the meat was roasted beforehand, it does not give off an aroma when brought up to the fire.

he did not break the leg but pierced it and hung from it. The common practice among flayers is to break one leg and place it inside the other leg; when he flayed the burnt-offering he did not do so, but made a hole in both knees of the animal and hung it on a hook inserted in the hole, with its hind legs upward. The reason he did so was so that the animal would remain hanging even after he cut up the first leg (Tosafot Yom Tov, Tamid 4:2, in the name of the commentator).
and if it was a bull he flays it without hanging. Because of its weight he did not hang it (Arukh HaShulchan 74:20).
and he flays until he reaches the breast. From the legs (hanging above) downward, to the breast.
the lower legs. The lower part of the animal's four legs.
and gave them to another. Another priest. The priests who received the parts of the animal would bring them up to the altar, as explained below in halakhah 10.
and completed the flaying. From the breast to the neck.

and he tore open the heart and removed its blood. He opened the chest opposite the heart and tore the heart open so that the blood gathered in it would come out (Radbaz; some explained that he did not tear open the chest but inserted his hand through the place of slaughter up to the heart, Tiferet Yisrael, Tamid 4:2).
and he cut off the forelegs. The upper part of the front legs.
he went up etc.. For the animal is hanging upside down with its legs up.
he went up to the right leg, cut it off, and gave it to another. To the same priest who also received the head (below halakhah 11).
and the two testicles with it. He cut off the upper part of the right hind leg in such a way that the two testicles (in a male offering) were cut off with it.
and afterwards he tears open the animal. The animal's belly.
the fat. The animal's fat (the fat covering the internal organs).

and he places it on the head above the place of slaughter. The priest holding the head would hold it so that its place of slaughter faced up (below halakhah 10), and on it the flayer would place the fat to cover the place of slaughter (which was soiled with blood), so the head would be brought up to the altar in a respectful manner (Bavli, Yoma 26a).
the innards. The organs of the digestive system.

they rinse it in the rinsing house as much as needed. They rinse it several times until it is completely clean, in the special chamber for rinsing the innards located in the south of the Temple court (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:17).
the intestines. The other digestive organs besides the stomach.

and they rinse them on marble tables between the pillars. Between the pillars on which they hung and flayed the animals. The pillars and tables were in the slaughter house, which was north of the altar (see Mishnah, Shekalim 6:4, Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:14).
he goes. The priest who received them, to bring them up the ramp.
and rinses them in water. To clean them of the waste they contain (and together with the innards he would rinse the lower legs, Gra's commentary to Tamid 4:2).
with diluted wine. Wine mixed with water.
the stomach. In which there is a lot of waste.
and he separated the lung from the liver and the lobe of the liver from the liver. He separated from the liver the lung and the caudate lobe of the liver (see above 1:18).
and he does not move the liver from its place. For it is taken with the right flank (and the lung is taken with the neck, and the lobe of the liver with the tail-end).
and he cuts open the breast. He cut around the breast and detached it from its attachment to the sides and the ribs.
to the right side. The meat and ribs on the right side of the animal.
and he cuts and goes down along the spine but does not touch the spine. He cut the flank right next to the backbone but without touching it (for the spine was taken with the left flank).

until he reaches two soft ribs. The two ribs adjacent to the neck. He cut the flank below those ribs, which were taken together with the neck, as explained in the next halakhah (and similarly he left the two soft ribs on the other side attached to the tail-end, as explained in the next halakhah).
the neck. The neck.
he left on it two ribs on this side and two ribs on that side. The two soft ribs adjacent to the neck on the right and the left.
and the windpipe. The trachea.
and he left on it two soft ribs above. The two ribs closest to the tail.
and two soft ribs below. The two ribs closest to the neck.
and the spine is with it and the spleen hangs from it. The backbone and the spleen remained attached to the left flank.
the tail-end. The rear end of the animal, the end of the spine next to the tail (Rosh, Tamid 31b).
he cut it off. From the left leg.
and the fat tail. The tail of the fat-tailed sheep.
and the fat tail, the lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with it. All of these were attached to the tail-end (and so too the two soft ribs on both sides, the commentator on Tamid 31a).
and in this order they flay and cut up every animal burnt-offering. The division of the limbs in this way is the division for all kinds of animals offered as burnt-offerings
,. Even for the largest species of animals (see below halakhah 19).
how many carry. How many priests carry the limbs to the ramp.
from the flock. A lamb or goat (excluding a lamb in its second year, which is considered a ram and whose law is detailed below in halakhah 17).
the first with the head and the leg. The first priest holds the head and the right hind leg.

in his right hand. In the priest's right hand. The priest would hold the animal's head with its face turned inward toward his arm, its horns between the fingers of his hand, and its place of slaughter (its neck) facing up. On top of the place of slaughter lay the animal's fat.
and the place of its skin outward. The lower side of the leg from which the skin is flayed faces outward.
and the fat tail hangs between his fingers. The fat tail hangs down from the tail-end between the priest's fingers.
and the lobe of the liver and the two kidneys with it. With the tail-end.
and the place of their skin outward. Of the tail-end and the leg.
and its ribs between his fingers. The four ribs (two on each side) that were attached to the neck were held in the priest's fingers.
placed in the bowl. In the dish.
ram. See above 1:14.
and if it was a ram, the fine flour is two and the wine is two. For its libations are larger than those of a lamb and goat (above 2:4).
and the second and third carry the right leg. Two priests carry the leg together.
the two forelegs by two. Each priest carried one of the front legs.
and why do they not divide the large limb of a bull into parts. So that each priest would carry a smaller piece by himself.
in what case is this said. That the pieces are carried by a fixed number of priests according to the type of animal.

but with individual burnt-offerings, if they wish to carry its pieces with fewer or more than these, they carry them. But the cutting up is done in the manner described above (Radbaz, Arukh HaShulchan 74:28).
and he turns to the surrounding ledge and comes to the southeast corner. As he goes up for sprinkling the blood of the sin-offering (above 5:10).
he pinches its head opposite its nape and separates. He cuts with his fingernail behind its neck and separates the head from the body (see below halakhah 23).
and squeezes out. He presses it against the wall of the altar and thereby squeezes the blood onto it.
above the line in the middle of the altar. The red line (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 2:9).

and he brings the place of its pinching near the altar. He brings the place of the pinching near the altar in order to put on it some of the salt that lay on the top of the altar (She'arei Heichal, Zevachim 160). Some explain that he would press its neck again to the wall of the altar to squeeze out the remaining blood in it (Likkutei Halakhot, Zevachim 64b).
and absorbs it in salt. He makes the salt absorb into its flesh.
the crop and the skin on it, in his hand with the feathers. He removed with his hands the crop with the skin covering it and the feathers on the skin.
and the entrails that come out with it. Together with the crop he removed the intestines attached to it and drawn after it as he takes it out.
and threw them to the place of the ashes. A place east of the ramp where they would put the ash of the removal of the ashes (Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 2:12).
and he tears it with its wings with his hand. He cuts and opens the body of the bird by hand from its back next to its spine.
and he does not need to separate. To separate the bird's body into two parts.
after the squeezing out of the blood. In the services after the squeezing out of the blood.
how is it pinched. See further below 7:8.
he cuts and goes down with the fingernail opposite the nape. He cuts with his fingernail behind the neck.
if he wished to go back and forth. To pinch the bird by moving the fingernail right and left across the nape.
he presses and goes down with the fingernail. By pressing inward.

and if the windpipe and gullet were displaced, he need not be concerned. Even if the signs of slaughter (windpipe and gullet) moved from their place, the pinching is valid (unlike slaughter, where displacement of the signs disqualifies, Hilchot Shechitah 3:14).

and he cuts the spine and the neck vertebra without most of the flesh etc.. When he cuts the neck vertebrae he must take care not to cut also most of the flesh over the vertebrae, since in such a case the bird is considered dead, like a carcass while alive, and pinching the signs no longer helps it (there 3:19).

and he must cut both signs in the burnt-offering. Most of the windpipe and the gullet (Commentary on the Mishnah, Zevachim 6:6; unlike the sin-offering, where cutting most of one sign suffices, below 7:6).
from the sides. From the sides of the neck.
he strangled. Killed in a way that is not slaughter (or pinching).
and the whole nape is valid for pinching. The entire back part of the neck.
in their commandment as stated in the Torah. Leviticus chapters 4-5.
he slaughters and gives the blood as we have explained. Slaughter at the north of the altar (above 5:2-3), and application of the blood on the four horns of the altar above (above 5:7).
and separates the sacrificial fats. Removes from the animal the parts that are offered on the altar (above 1:18).
and salts them. As with everything offered on the altar (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 5:11).
and throws them onto the fires. On the fire pile on the altar.
and if he wished to put the sacrificial fats in a vessel when he throws them onto the altar, he may. And he is not required to carry and throw them by hand.
is eaten by male priests in the Temple court. Below 10:3.
the sin-offerings that are burned. The bull and goat of Yom Kippur, the bull for an unwitting communal error, the bull of the anointed priest, and the goats of idolatry (above 1:16).
as we have explained. Above 5:11-16.
he tears them open. He tears open their bellies to remove the sacrificial fats.

and they cut them up there like the pieces of the burnt-offering, in their skin. They cut the flesh of the sin-offerings that are burned in the way the flesh of the burnt-offering is cut (above 6:5-9), but without flaying the skin (see also above 5:18).
in the place of the ashes. In the special place for burning the sin-offerings that are burned (below halakhah 4).
disqualified sacred offerings. Most holy offerings (meat and sacrificial fats) that were disqualified (through impurity and the like).

and the sacrificial fats of lesser sacrifices that were disqualified. The sacrificial fats of lesser sacrifices are burned on the altar in the Temple court, so their burning when disqualified is also in the Temple court.
and the bulls and goats of the sin-offerings that are burned, if a disqualification occurred in them. While they are still in the Temple court.
that went out of the Temple court before the time came for them to go out. Before the sprinkling of the blood.
or the meat was left overnight. The meat remained the whole night in the Temple court and was not taken out to the burning place (see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:3 and the Pesakim VeShitot there).
or the sacrificial fats were left overnight. And were not burned on the altar.
when they are burned as their commandment requires. According to their proper law and not because of a disqualification.
by a non-priest. One who is not a priest.
and with gevavah. Straw mixed with manure gathered from the fields.
fire of any kind. All kinds of fire.
to exclude lime and hot ash. Boiling lime and hot ash, which burn by heat and not by fire.
he pinches it... as we have explained. Above 6:23.
at the southwest corner. From below (below halakhah 10).

and he goes down with his fingernail until he cuts the signs or most of one of them. As with the slaughter of a bird, where cutting most of one sign suffices (Hilchot Shechitah 1:9; and unlike the bird burnt-offering, where he must cut both signs, above 6:23).
and he does not separate the head from the body. He does not separate the head from the body (unlike the bird burnt-offering, ibid.).
and sprinkles of its blood on the wall of the altar. He holds the body and head of the bird and shakes the blood onto the altar (not with his finger or from a vessel).
below the middle. Below the red line.

and the remainder of the blood is squeezed out on the base. Following the sprinkling, he would bring the bird close to the wall of the altar so the blood would be squeezed from the bird and flow along the altar wall to the base (Arukh HaShulchan 77:9; and see Even HaAzel, who said that the arrival of the sprinkled blood at the base is itself the squeezing out).

from which we learn that the application is on a wall whose remainder is squeezed out on a base, and this is the lower wall. From the verse we learn that the blood of the bird sin-offering must be applied on the wall of the altar from which the blood will fall to the base. That wall is the surrounding wall (located above the base) and most of it is in the lower part of the altar, therefore the blood of the bird sin-offering is applied on the lower part of the altar.
and the altar has nothing of it except its blood. None of its flesh is burned on the altar.
and the rest. All the flesh.
like the flesh of the animal sin-offering. Below 10:3.

how does he hold the bird sin-offering etc.. The priest holds the bird on the back of his hand (and not in the palm of his hand). He holds the bird's legs between two of his fingers, and its wings between his other two fingers. With his thumb he stretches the bird's neck toward the palm of his hand, so that the bird's nape faced outward, and thus he pinched the bird.
and its two wings. Its two wings.
if he changed and held it in any way. If he held the bird in a different manner, in any way at all.
and any place on the altar is valid for its pinching. Not only at the southwest corner where its commandment ab initio is, but even above or in other places around the altar.
and if he sprinkled in any place, it is valid. Even above.
provided that he put a little of the blood of life below. On the lower part of the altar.
of the blood of life. The blood through which the life departs (and it is the blood of which one must sprinkle on the altar).
the southwest corner etc.. The southwest corner of the altar in the upper half (above the red line), and in the lower half.
the bird sin-offering. Its pinching and the sprinkling of its blood (above halakhah 6).
and the presentation of the meal-offerings. Bringing the meal-offering near the corner before the taking of the handful (below 12:6).
and the remainder of the blood... that they pour on it. Above 5:6, 5:10.
the water libation that is poured on the festival. On the festival of Sukkot, with the libations of the morning tamid offering (Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 10:6).
and the wine libation of the libations. Above 2:1.

and the bird burnt-offering when it is plentiful etc.. Usually the bird burnt-offering was done at the southeast corner above (above 6:20), and when there were many burnt-offerings and there was no room there, they would do it at the southwest corner.

they go up by the right and go around and come down by the left. They go up and turn to the right side of the altar (toward the southeast), and do not return the way they came but go around the entire altar and come down on its other side (southwest).
for one of these three things. The water libation, the wine libation, and the bird burnt-offering.
they go up and turn left to the corner. In going up to the altar they turn left directly to the southwest corner.
and do their work, and return by the heel. After they finish their work at this corner, they do not continue around the whole altar but return the way they came.

one who pours water or wine, when he goes around the altar etc.. Although the one pouring would turn to his left, he was permitted to go around the whole altar (by way of his right) without the wine or water, and when he reached the corner others (who had not gone around) would give him the wine or water.
and if he did not go around etc.. If he does not wish to go around the whole altar, he turns to his left and arrives immediately at the southwest corner.
sackcloth. A fabric of goat hair and the like.
hard leather is like wood. It has the law of a wooden vessel (below halakhah 4).
the sin-offering that is burned. Above 1:16.
that had its time of fitness. That the sacrifice was done validly.
that was left overnight. That the sacrifice was disqualified by being left overnight (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 3:7).
and that went out of the Temple court. That the blood or meat went out of the Temple court (there 1:31, 1:35).
and fit for laundering. A soft garment that can be cleaned by rubbing it in water.
because it is not fit to receive impurity. For what is made of sea animals does not receive impurity (Hilchot Kelim 1:3).
before it was flayed it does not require laundering. For it is not considered a vessel at all.
that spurted from the neck. From the animal's neck before it reached the vessel.
from the horn of the altar. After the blood was sprinkled on it.

that the blood was spilled on the floor and he gathered it. The blood spilled from the animal's neck onto the floor and from there he gathered it into a vessel (but if it spilled from the vessel and he gathered it, it requires laundering, Radbaz).
in a service vessel. Vessels used for the holy service in the Temple.
and it has enough for sprinkling. Enough blood that one can sprinkle from it (see above 4:8).
he gave the four applications. That one must give of the sin-offering on the horns of the altar (above 5:7).

from the remainder of the blood etc.. The blood that remained in the vessel after the applications are given is poured on the base (above 5:10). The blood of this sin-offering was already sprinkled and is therefore no longer fit for sprinkling and does not require laundering.

and likewise with the sin-offerings that are burned, if it spattered from his finger etc.. The blood of the inner sin-offerings is sprinkled by dipping the finger into the vessel containing the blood. If the blood spattered from the finger onto the garment before the priest sprinkled the blood, the garment requires laundering; but if it spattered onto the garment after the sprinkling, from the remains of blood on the finger, the garment does not require laundering, since this blood is unfit for further sprinkling (above 5:8).
for it was not absorbed in it. The second blood was not absorbed in the garment.
until no trace of it remains. Until the blood is not visible on the garment at all.
the seven cleansers that are passed over a stain. Cleaning agents used on a garment that has a red mark on it to determine whether it is blood or dye (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 9:36-37).
they are passed over the blood of a sin-offering. In addition to laundering it in water.
scouring and rinsing. Below halakhah 12.
and likewise a vessel in which it was cooked etc.. They have the same law.
a vessel into which he poured something boiling. He poured into it a boiling dish of sin-offering meat.
scouring. Thorough washing of the vessel (Commentary on the Mishnah, Zevachim 11:8).
and rinsing. Pouring water as additional cleaning, without rubbing the vessel (there).
with diluted wine. Wine mixed with water.
like the scouring of a cup and its rinsing. One need not be meticulous to remove every trace completely (there).
and the spit. Used for roasting.
and the grill. A metal grate on which meat is roasted.
he purges them in hot water over the fire. He draws out the absorbed fat in them by putting them in a pot on the fire containing boiling water (see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 17:4).
after its blood was sprinkled properly. For then the meat of the sin-offering was permitted to be eaten (below 11:4).
if he roasted the meat in a clay oven. While it is suspended in the air and its walls do not absorb the taste of the sin-offering (Bavli, Zevachim 95b).
immediately after eating. After the eating and close to it (Radbaz).
and he does not leave them until the time of the second eating. He does not leave them without scouring and rinsing until the next time he eats.
and he cooks, repeats and does a third time immediately. He may cook several times in a row without scouring and rinsing between them.
and scours and rinses at the end of eating. At the end of the last eating (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Zevachim 11:7).
and earthenware vessels. That were not fired in a kiln.
it is eaten like it and in its sanctity. The food must be eaten according to the laws of eating a sin-offering (see below 10:3, 10:7).
when it was absorbed in it. The meat of the sin-offering was absorbed in the food that touched it.
in a thin cake. Thin bread.
if there is in them a giving of taste. If the sacred offerings give taste to non-sacred food, or the most holy offerings give taste to lesser sacred offerings.
everything is eaten as the more stringent of them. According to the eating laws of the stricter of the two foods.

and the vessel requires scouring and rinsing, and everything follows the more stringent of them in every respect. For example, in a case where he cooked in a vessel a sin-offering and lesser sacrifices, the vessel requires scouring and rinsing specifically in the Temple court. But if he cooked in it only lesser sacrifices, he may rinse the vessel even outside the Temple court (Chazon Dovid, Zevachim 10:6).
and if one did not give taste to the other. If the stricter did not give taste to the lighter.
but the vessel requires scouring and rinsing. Like any vessel in which sacred offerings were cooked (above halakhah 14).
he returns it to the Temple court and launders it there. As above in halakhah 1.

if it became impure outside the Temple court, what does he do. For it is forbidden to bring impurity into the Temple (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:16), yet on the other hand the garment must be laundered in the Temple court.
he tears it so that it becomes pure. He tears most of the garment and thereby it becomes pure.
and he must leave in it a whole piece of the size of a cloth. He does not tear the whole garment but leaves in it a whole piece the size of a kerchief (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 29:1).
he must launder a garment. And when it is torn entirely it is not considered a garment.
impure by rabbinic decree because of the size of a cloth that remains in it. Hilchot Kelim 23:11.
and one who tears it is flogged, as we have explained. Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 9:3.

he brings it in less than three, less than three fingerbreadths. In this way (bringing in a small part of the garment that is less than the measure for garment impurity), there is no prohibition of bringing impurity into the Temple court.
and launders it inside etc.. He brings a small part of the cloak into the Temple court and launders it, and then brings another part and launders it, until all the blood is laundered out.
he brings it in and breaks it inside. Above halakhah 11.

he pierces it with a hole the size of a small root so that it becomes pure etc.. When he makes a small hole the vessel becomes pure of its impurity but is still considered a vessel; if he makes a larger hole it is not considered a vessel at all (Hilchot Kelim 19:2).

the size of a small root. Its size is less than an olive's bulk (Hilchot Terumot 5:15; and see Lechem Mishneh and Even HaAzel as to why a hole the size of an olive's bulk is not needed here, which is the hole by which a vessel becomes pure of receiving impurity, as explained in Hilchot Kelim there).
and only vessels are broken inside, not fragments of vessels. And not shards of vessels.
he brings it in, scours it and rinses it inside. Above halakhah 11.
he makes a breach in it. He makes a large hole in it.
until it becomes pure. Hilchot Kelim 11:1-2.
and he hammers it out until the breach is closed. He flattens the vessel and closes the hole.
and it returns to the form of vessels. The vessel becomes a complete vessel again.
a definite guilt-offering... a suspensive guilt-offering. See above 1:6.

he slaughters it and sprinkles the blood as we have explained. Slaughter in the Temple court at the north of the altar (above 5:2), and sprinkling of the blood, two applications that are four (there halakhah 6).
and flays and removes the sacrificial fats... like the sin-offering. See above 7:1.
the guilt-offering of a leper. Which the leper brings on the day of his purification (Hilchot Shegagot 10:3).

there is a difference in the receiving of its blood, as will be explained in Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah. 4:2. There it is explained that two priests receive its blood: one in a vessel, for sprinkling on the altar; and the second in his hand, to apply of this blood on the leper.
kinds. Types.
communal peace-offerings. The lambs of Atzeret (above 1:4).
and the three individual peace-offerings. Below halakhah 5.

he slaughters and sprinkles the blood as we have explained. Slaughter in the Temple court at the north of the altar (above 5:2), and sprinkling of the blood, two applications that are four (there halakhah 6).
because they are most holy offerings, as we have explained. Above 1:17.

such as the peace-offerings of the festival pilgrimage and rejoicing. Offerings that those who go up for the festival are obligated to bring (Hilchot Chagigah 1:1). This category also includes an ordinary peace-offering brought as a vow or voluntary offering.

the peace-offerings that the nazirite brings on the day of completion. When he finishes the days of his naziriteship, and together with this offering he brings twenty loaves (Hilchot Nezirut 8:1, below halakhah 23).
he slaughters and sprinkles the blood as we have explained. He slaughters anywhere in the Temple court (above 5:4), and sprinkles two applications that are four (there halakhah 6).
he cuts up the meat. He cuts it into pieces.
and separates the breast and the right thigh. He separates the breast and the (hind) leg from the other pieces; these parts are given to the priests (below halakhah 11).
before the Lord, at the east. In the eastern part of the Temple court.
and likewise anything requiring waving is waved at the east. See also Hilchot Sotah 3:15, Hilchot Temidin U'Musafin 7:12, 8:11, Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 4:2.
he moves it forward and back. He shakes it in the four directions (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 5:5).

he takes one out of ten of the bread that comes with it. With the thanksgiving-offering they bring forty loaves of four kinds (below halakhot 17-18), and the priest would take one loaf of each kind (below halakhah 21).
and he waves everything by the hands of the owners, as we have explained. Above halakhah 6.
the fats. The fats of the sacrificial portions (above 1:18).
and the two kidneys and the lobe of the liver. Sacrificial portions (there).
in the Women's Court. Which was east of the Temple court, where there was a special chamber for cooking the nazirite's ram (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:7-8).
the cooked shoulder of the ram. The priest takes out from the parts of the ram that were cooked the right foreleg.
with one out of ten of the bread that comes with it. With the nazirite's ram the nazirite brings twenty loaves of two kinds, and the priest takes one loaf of each kind (below halakhah 23).
as we have explained. Above halakhah 6.
whoever sees the ground etc.. The lower part of the animal's body that is above the ground when the animal stands, from the neck to the animal's stomach.
and which is the foreleg etc.. See also Hilchot Bikkurim 9:18.
from the joint of the elbow to the palm of the hand. From the joint at the end of the upper arm bone attached to the body, downward to the hooves (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Chullin 4:6, 10:4).

for they are two limbs joined together. The foreleg includes two bones joined together (and it is possible to explain that these words refer to "palm of the hand" and explain that it means the animal's hoof, which is made of two bones attached to each other).
and opposite it in the hind leg is the thigh. The same part in the right hind leg is the thigh.
and the priests do not acquire. Do not acquire and are not able to eat.

one is not liable to death and a fifth, as with terumah. For a non-priest who eats terumah deliberately is liable to death at the hands of Heaven, and if inadvertently pays the value of the terumah plus a fifth (Hilchot Terumot 6:6).

and it does not render forbidden by mixture like terumah. When terumah gets mixed into fewer than a hundred parts of non-sacred produce, the mixture has the law of terumah, permitted to eat only to priests and in purity (there 13:2). The thanksgiving loaves of the priests that got mixed are nullified in a majority, like other prohibitions (Radbaz, Kesef Mishneh).

the rest of the bread is eaten by the owners like the thanksgiving-offering of an Israelite etc.. Like the loaves of an Israelite's thanksgiving-offering, and it is not burned like a priest's meal-offering (below 12:9).
by all of them. For all of them.
unlike with laying of hands. For all lay hands one after another (above 3:9).
the priest waves, if her sacrifice requires waving and she is unfit for waving. The priest waves all the wavings together with the owners, and when they cannot wave he waves alone.
except the suspected adulteress. She waves her meal-offering (Hilchot Sotah 3:15).
and the nazirite woman. She waves the raised portion of her nazirite's ram (Hilchot Nezirut 8:4).

and waving precedes presentation everywhere. Meal-offerings must be presented at the corner of the altar before they are burned, and the meal-offering of the suspected adulteress and the omer meal-offering must also be waved (below 12:6), and the waving must be done before the presentation.
twenty issarons of fine flour. About forty-two liters.
leaven. Sour dough of water and flour used to make other dough rise.
enough to make it leaven. In an amount sufficient to leaven the fine flour.
and he places it in the measure and fills the measure. He puts the leaven into the issaron measuring vessel and fills the rest of the measure with fine flour.

even though it will end up deficient or in excess because of the leaven, which is sometimes thick and hard and sometimes soft. For leaven may be dense or airy (according to the ratio of flour and water in it). As a result the total amount of fine flour in the issaron (made up of the meal-offering's fine flour and the leaven) will be more or less than if the entire issaron were fine flour without leaven.
loaves baked in an oven. Mixed with oil before being kneaded with water and baked (below halakhah 21).
wafers. Kneaded with water only, and after baking in the oven smeared with oil (there).
fried. Fried in plenty of oil.
he scalds it with boiling water. He pours boiling water on the fine flour.
and afterwards he fries it in oil on a pan and the like. He fries the fine flour in a vessel in which it floats in oil.
sponge cakes. Made of dough soft like a sponge and fried in oil.

and this is the frying mentioned everywhere. And in this way, with a great deal of oil, the griddle-cake meal-offering is also made, of which it says "fried you shall bring it" (Leviticus 6:14; Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 9:3, and see below 13:2).
in half a log of oil. About one hundred fifty cc.
a law given to Moses at Sinai. A tradition of the Oral Torah.
the loaves... and the wafers. See also below 13:8.
he mixes. He mixes.
he kneads. With lukewarm water (there).
four loaves. One loaf of each kind.
provided that he separates their loaf... while it is dough. The bread given to the priest must be separated from the dough and baked separately.
one of each offering. Whole.
a broken piece. A cut piece.
he takes six issarons and two-thirds of an issaron. About fourteen liters.
a revi'it. A quarter of a log, about seventy-five cc.
they hold each other up. He cannot bring one of them without bringing the rest.
and the making of the bread. Its preparation.
that he sprinkle their blood as we have explained. One application opposite the base (above 5:17).
the flesh of the firstborn is eaten by the priests. Hilchot Bechorot 1:2.
and the rest of the flesh of the tithe is eaten by its owners. There 4:4.
it is eaten by those enrolled for it. Only by those who were enrolled for the offering (Hilchot Korban Pesach 2:1).
according to its laws, as will be explained in Hilchot HaPesach. According to the laws of eating the Passover offering (there chapters 8-10).
"and they shall eat those by which atonement was made". Through the eating the atonement is achieved.
the remainders of the meal-offerings. From the meal-offerings that an Israelite brings, a handful is burned on the altar, and the rest of the meal-offering is eaten by the priests (below 12:9).
by male priests. By male priests, even minors (below halakhah 17).

and if they were eaten in the Sanctuary, they were eaten. And their eating counts as the eating of a commandment. And in a time of need it is permitted to eat them in the Sanctuary even ab initio (Commentary on the Mishnah, Zevachim 6:1).

as it is said, "every meal-offering of theirs and every sin-offering of theirs and every guilt-offering of theirs etc., in the Holy of Holies you shall eat it". From here we learn that in a time of need one may eat them even in the Sanctuary, which the verse here calls "Holy of Holies" (Bavli, Zevachim 63a; and see Ibn Ezra on Numbers 18:10).
communal peace-offerings are like the sin-offering and guilt-offering, as we have explained. Above 5:3, 9:4.
and females. A priest's daughter (provided she did not marry a non-priest, Hilchot Terumot 6:7).
the raised portion of a thanksgiving-offering and the raised portion of a nazirite's ram. Above 9:13.
the breast and thigh of peace-offerings. Which are given to the priests (above 9:11).
to the priests' slaves. The Canaanite slaves.
and to their wives. The wife of a priest, even if she is not a priest's daughter.
like terumah. Hilchot Terumot 6:1-3.
in the whole city. Jerusalem.
"the breast of waving and the thigh of the raised portion". And the continuation of the verse: "you shall eat in a pure place".

the whole camp of Israel, whose counterpart for the generations is Jerusalem. In the time of the Tabernacle, the camp of Israel was defined as a "pure place", and after the Temple was built Jerusalem is considered the place corresponding in rank to the camp of Israel (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 7:11).

and the same applies to the tithe and the Passover offering. The tithe and Passover offerings are also considered lesser sacrifices (above 1:17), and the eating of their meat by the owners is done inside Jerusalem.

and the windows and the thickness of the wall are like inside. The windows in the wall of Jerusalem and the top of the wall are considered inside Jerusalem, and one may eat lesser sacrifices in them (and see also Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 2:16; Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 6:9 and the Pesakim VeShitot there).
for two days and one night. The night between them.
until the pillar of dawn rises. The beginning of the lighting of the east before sunrise (about an hour and a fifth before it, Commentary on the Mishnah, Berakhot 1:1).
and to keep far from transgression. See also Hilchot Keriat Shema 1:9, above 4:2.

the Sages said that they are eaten only until midnight. Since it is difficult to determine when dawn begins, the Sages enacted a decree here; but with peace-offerings, which are eaten until sunset (above halakhah 6), they made no decree, for it is easy to tell when the sun sets (Tosafot, Zevachim 57b).
the circumcised. Who were circumcised.

even if his sun has set and he has not brought his atonement, he does not eat of sacred offerings. An impure person who immersed completes the purification process only after the sun sets. And if he is among the impure who are obligated to bring a sacrifice for their impurity (zavim, lepers, a woman after childbirth), he is not fully purified until after he brings his sacrifice, and it is forbidden for him to eat sacred offerings until then (see Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:7).
and the tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and it is not clear whether he is male or female. [Note: in the Commentary on the Mishnah the Rambam vocalizes this word: tumtom.]
he is forbidden to eat sacred offerings, since he is possibly uncircumcised. For he may be male, and he was not circumcised.
the androgynos. One who has both male and female sexual organs.
it seems to me that he eats lesser sacrifices. In a case where he was circumcised. But from most holy offerings he does not eat, since he is not definitely male.
in any food. To eat them in whatever manner they wish.

shaluk. Lightly boiled in water without spices (note of Rabbi Y. Kafih on the Commentary on the Mishnah, Berakhot 6:8; and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 10:11, Hilchot Nedarim 9:1). Some explain that shaluk means well cooked (Rashi, Nedarim 49a and elsewhere; and see Meiri there, who says the word is explained in both senses, depending on context).

so that they do not bring the terumah to disqualification. After the time of their eating the sacred offerings become disqualified from eating (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 18:9-10), and if they cook with them spices of terumah and delay eating the dish, the spice will be disqualified when the sacred offerings are disqualified.
and the bones that remain. And are not fit for eating (Radbaz, Kesef Mishneh).
a small eating. A little food.
so that it be eaten with satiety. From satiety.
so that it not be eaten with revulsion. So that they not eat it after they are already sick of eating more.
a sin-offering or guilt-offering. Most holy offerings eaten by male priests in the Temple court for a day and a night.
with the raised portion of a thanksgiving-offering or of a nazirite's ram. Lesser sacrifices eaten by male and female priests throughout Jerusalem for a day and a night.

because it reduces those who eat them and the place of their eating. When they are cooked with the sin-offering, the law of a sin-offering applies to them, and they become forbidden to females and outside the Temple court.
a firstborn, or with the breast and thigh of peace-offerings. Eaten by male and female priests for two days and one night.
a raised portion of peace-offerings of yesterday. That were slaughtered and offered yesterday and are eaten until sunset of this day.
a sin-offering and guilt-offering of the day. Which are eaten also at night.

for it reduces those who eat them and the place of their eating and the time of their eating. The sin-offering and guilt-offering reduce the eaters and the place of the raised portion of the peace-offerings, and the raised portion of the peace-offerings reduces the time of the sin-offering and guilt-offering.
piggul. A sacrifice disqualified by an intention outside its time or outside its place (in the general sense of the term "piggul", see for example the Rosh's commentary, Nedarim 10:2).
nothar. Meat of a sacrifice whose time for eating has passed.

that was cooked with other pieces. And the forbidden pieces were removed from the dish, and their amount at the outset was not in a measure that forbids the mixture in other prohibitions (Commentary on the Mishnah, Orlah 2:16).

forbidden to non-priests and permitted to priests. Because of the severity of the prohibition for a non-priest to eat sacred offerings, they were not permitted to eat the other pieces even when the sacred meat was nullified in the mixture. However, with regard to priests, since the meat was originally permitted to them for eating, even when it became forbidden as piggul and nothar, its prohibition is not as severe and it is nullified (there).
meat of desire. Non-sacred meat (permitted for eating to the impure).

the meat of desire is forbidden to the impure and permitted to the pure. Even when the meat of desire was the majority, it does not nullify the sacred meat, so the dish must be eaten in purity. And the dish is permitted for eating to pure non-priests, and in the case of most holy offerings it is permitted only to pure priests (Commentary on the Mishnah, Orlah 2:17).
the verse speaks in all of these only of one who is fit. It does not speak of the priest who actually performed the services of the sacrifice, but of all the priests fit to perform these services.
